title: Progressive dry cough and weight loss in a retired builder
desc: This station is a focused chronic cough history and respiratory examination of a 75-year-old retired builder in general practice. He has months of dry cough, exertional breathlessness, weight loss, hoarseness and a dull upper chest pain, and was exposed to asbestos in the late 1960s and 1970s. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, chest X-ray and bloods, recognises a right apical lung mass suspicious for lung cancer, arranges an urgent CT and specialist referral, explains the result honestly and safety-nets.
focus: Chronic cough: a red-flag and occupational history, then recognising and urgently referring a suspicious apical lung mass
stem: You are a third-year medical student on placement in a general practice. James Davidson is a 75-year-old retiree who has come to see you because of a cough. Your supervising GP is available in the next room.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Davidson and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, the report of his chest X-ray and his blood results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are James Davidson, a 75-year-old retired builder. You are polite, a bit puzzled, and your voice is slightly croaky. You are comfortable sitting still, though walking in from the waiting room made you cough a little. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "I've had this cough for months now, doctor, and it just isn't going away."

The cough (give only when asked):

  • Onset: it came on gradually, maybe 4 or 5 months ago. You can't name a day it started.
  • Course: it has been getting worse over the last few months.
  • Character: dry. No phlegm and no blood, ever.
  • Timing: you cough regularly through the whole day. It is not worse first thing in the morning and does not wake you at night.
  • Better: resting. Worse: exercise and walking.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • Breathlessness: you get short of breath walking. You and your wife used to walk most days, but now you struggle to go for walks because of the breathlessness and the cough. You have to stop after a couple of hundred metres. Fine at rest.
  • Chest pain: a dull ache in the upper right side of your chest, below the collarbone. It has come on over the last month or two and is there most of the time, about 3 out of 10. It is not sharp, not worse when you breathe in, and not brought on by exertion. It does not spread to your neck, jaw or arm.
  • Weight: you haven't weighed yourself, but your wife says you look thinner and your trousers are looser. Your appetite is "not what it was".
  • Voice: your voice has become hoarse over the past month or two.
  • Energy: you feel tired and flat all the time (lethargy).
  • Heart failure questions: you sleep on one pillow and can lie flat. You don't wake up at night gasping. No ankle swelling.
  • Airways: no wheeze, and no cough that is worse in the mornings.
  • Infection: no fever, chills or shivers. No phlegm. No sharp pain on breathing in. No one around you has been sick.
  • TB questions: no overseas travel and no night sweats or fevers. No known contact with TB.
  • Other exposures (only if asked): no pet birds or pigeons, no farm or mouldy hay exposure, and no medicines other than ramipril and the multivitamin (never taken amiodarone, methotrexate or nitrofurantoin).
  • Only if asked directly: no pain or tingling down the arm, no weakness in your hand, no drooping eyelid, no trouble swallowing, no swelling of your face or neck, no bone pain, no headaches, no confusion.

Past medical history: high blood pressure. Nothing else. No lung problems before this. No previous chest X-rays that you remember.

Medications: ramipril for your blood pressure. You have taken it for years, and you can't remember the dose. No recent change in dose. You also take a daily multivitamin. If asked about drugs: "I had some marijuana as a teenager, nothing since."

Allergies: none known.

Family history: your father had type 2 diabetes. No one in the family has had lung disease or cancer that you know of.

Social history:

  • You have never smoked cigarettes. You don't drink alcohol.
  • You are a retired builder. You started as an apprentice builder at 15 in the late 1960s and worked in building through the 1970s. If the candidate only asks about your job, just say "I was a builder."
  • Only if asked specifically about asbestos, or about dust, fibres or hazardous materials at work: "Yes, there was a lot of asbestos back then. The company I worked for actually went bankrupt after paying compensation to workers for asbestos exposure."
  • You used to walk for exercise but can't now because of the breathlessness and cough.
  • You eat home-cooked meals.
  • You live with your wife, who is well and very supportive. You manage everything at home yourself.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are not sure what is going on. You are worried it might be the coronavirus. You would like to know what is causing the cough and get something to settle it.

Question to raise: if the candidate has not asked about your worries by the end of the history: "Do you think it's the coronavirus, doctor?"

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: thin older man, comfortable at rest, speaking in full sentences with a hoarse voice. Not cyanosed. No obvious pallor. Weight 68 kg, height 178 cm (BMI 21.5). The practice record shows 74 kg eight months ago.
  • Vital signs (10:05): HR 86 beats/min regular; BP 140/82 mmHg; RR 18/min; SpO2 95% on room air; temperature 36.6 °C.
  • Hands: no clubbing, no nicotine staining, no wasting of the small muscles of the hand, normal grip. Sensation normal if tested.
  • Face: no ptosis, pupils equal and reactive (no Horner's syndrome). No facial swelling or plethora.
  • Neck: trachea midline. JVP not raised and neck veins not distended. No cervical or supraclavicular lymph nodes.
  • Chest: expansion symmetrical. Percussion dull over the right apex (above the clavicle and in the first and second intercostal spaces anteriorly), resonant elsewhere. Breath sounds and vocal resonance reduced over the right apex. Vesicular breath sounds elsewhere. No crackles (in particular no fine bibasal crackles), no wheeze, no pleural rub.
  • Cardiovascular: heart sounds dual with no murmurs. No ankle or sacral oedema.
  • Abdomen and spine: no hepatomegaly. No spinal or rib tenderness.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as a third-year medical student, confirms the patient's identity, explains the purpose of the consultation and gains consent.
Opens with an open question, then focuses, and uses plain language throughout.
History
Characterises the cough:

kids.x: Onset and course: gradual onset about 4 to 5 months ago, worse over the last few months.
Asks about sputum and haemoptysis: dry, with no sputum and no blood.
Pattern: throughout the day, not mainly in the mornings or at night. Better with rest and worse with exercise.

check.x: Asks about breathlessness and its impact: short of breath on exertion, and he can no longer go for walks.
Asks about features of malignancy:

kids.x: Weight loss (his wife says he looks thinner, clothes looser), reduced appetite and lethargy.
Hoarse voice for the past month or two.
Chest pain: dull, upper right chest, constant, not pleuritic or exertional, not radiating.

check.x: Takes an occupational history and asks specifically about asbestos or hazardous dust exposure: a builder through the late 1960s and 1970s whose company went bankrupt after paying workers compensation for asbestos exposure.
check.d: The asbestos history is only given if asbestos or dust/hazardous exposure at work is asked about. 'What was your job?' alone does not earn this item.

check.x: Screens for the other causes of a chronic cough:
check.d: Credit each condition screened with at least two of the listed questions. Pulmonary fibrosis carries the most weight.

kids.x: Pulmonary fibrosis: progressive exertional breathlessness with a dry cough, linked to dust or asbestos exposure, with other exposures (for example birds or medicines).
Heart failure: orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, ankle swelling (none).
COPD or asthma: smoking history, morning cough, wheeze (none).
Pneumonia: fever, chills, sputum, pleuritic pain, sick contacts (none).
Tuberculosis: travel, night sweats, fevers, TB contact (none).

check.x: Takes the past medical, medication and allergy history:

kids.x: Medications: ramipril (dose unknown, taken for years, no recent change), with ACE inhibitor cough considered; daily multivitamin.

check.x: Takes a family history: father with type 2 diabetes; asks about lung disease or cancer in the family (none).
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Has never smoked tobacco (marijuana as a teenager only) and drinks no alcohol.
Lives with his wife with good support, independent at home, home-cooked meals, used to walk for exercise.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: he is unsure what is happening and worried it is the coronavirus.
Examination
General inspection: build and cachexia, hoarse voice, work of breathing, cyanosis, pallor. Measures his weight and compares it with the practice record (74 kg to 68 kg).
Requests a full set of vital signs, including SpO2.
Examines the hands for clubbing, nicotine staining and wasting of the small hand muscles.
Examines the face and neck: Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis), facial swelling, tracheal position, JVP, and cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes.
Examines the chest, including the apices: expansion, percussion and auscultation. Finds dullness and reduced breath sounds at the right apex, with no fine crackles.
Looks for heart failure and spread: heart sounds, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly, and spinal or rib tenderness.
Interpretation

Observations: normal at rest (SpO2 95% on room air), falling to SpO2 92% with HR 98 and RR 22 after a short walk. States he is not acutely unwell and can have an urgent outpatient work-up. Notes 6 kg (about 8%) weight loss in 8 months.
Chest X-ray: gives the spot diagnosis first, a right upper lobe (apical) opacity or mass about 6 cm across, consistent with an apical lung tumour.
check.d: Both the right upper lobe opacity and the words apical (superior sulcus) lung tumour are needed.

check.x: Chest X-ray: reads it systematically after the spot diagnosis and gives the relevant negatives. Trachea central, mediastinum and hila normal, no effusion, pleural plaques or interstitial change, heart size normal, costophrenic angles clear. The upper ribs are not fully assessed.
check.d: Accept the systematic read in the ISBAR assessment or in the diagnosis answer.

check.x: Bloods: mild normocytic anaemia, mild thrombocytosis, raised CRP and low albumin, in keeping with chronic disease. Corrected calcium and sodium are normal (no hypercalcaemia or hyponatraemia). eGFR 70 is adequate for contrast CT.

States the most likely diagnosis is primary lung cancer (superior sulcus or Pancoast tumour) until proven otherwise, with mesothelioma as an asbestos-related alternative, and that CT and a tissue diagnosis are needed. Justifies it with the asbestos exposure, weight loss, hoarseness, chest pain, breathlessness and the apical mass.
check.d: Full marks for primary lung cancer named as most likely with mesothelioma as an alternative, each justified. Asbestosis and the other differentials are marked in item 27. The critical standard is met by naming primary lung cancer (malignant apical mass) as most likely and stating that CT and tissue diagnosis are needed. Mesothelioma as an alternative is needed for full marks only.

check.x: Justifies the other differentials with the feature against each: asbestos-related pulmonary fibrosis (no clubbing, no crackles, no reticular change on the X-ray), ACE inhibitor cough (on ramipril for years, does not explain the mass or weight loss), heart failure (no orthopnoea, oedema or cardiomegaly), TB (no fevers, sweats, travel or cavitation).
Management
Arranges an urgent contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and upper abdomen, without letting it delay the referral.

Refers urgently, by phone and letter with the supervising GP, to a respiratory physician or lung cancer multidisciplinary team, to be seen within 2 weeks. The referral includes the asbestos history, X-ray and bloods.

States that antibiotics, or a trial off ramipril, must not delay the CT and referral, and that further staging and biopsy (for example PET-CT, CT-guided or bronchoscopic biopsy) will be arranged by the specialist team.
Explains the result honestly in plain language:

kids.x: The X-ray shows a shadow or lump at the top of the right lung that could be a cancer, possibly linked to his asbestos exposure; only a CT and biopsy can tell. Avoids both false reassurance and a definite cancer diagnosis.
Addresses the coronavirus worry: a cough building over months without fever is very unlikely to be coronavirus.
Checks understanding, invites questions and offers for his wife to attend.

check.x: Safety netting

Gives at least three specific red flags in plain words, each with the correct action, including:
  • severe or worsening breathlessness or noisy breathing (stridor) → 000
  • coughing up blood → 000 if more than a small amount, otherwise ED today
  • swelling of the face, neck or arm → ED today
  • new back or neck pain with weakness, numbness or tingling in the legs, or new trouble passing urine or controlling the bladder or bowels → call 000 or go to ED now
Separately: new pain, weakness or numbness in the arm or hand → call the practice the same day (prompt review, not an emergency).
check.d: Credit any three of the four listed red flags, each with the correct action. The arm or hand line is credited but not required. Also accept (not required): new, severe or different chest pain (000); fever or new confusion (ED today).

check.x: Arranges follow-up: GP review with the CT result within a week (with his wife), and asks him to call if he has not heard about the CT or specialist appointment.

part2.lead: Mr Davidson had a chest X-ray and blood tests at the imaging and pathology centre next door, and has come back to see you this afternoon. Here are his observations, the chest X-ray report and his blood results.
part2.patient:
When the candidate explains, Mr Davidson asks, if not already covered:

  • "So it's not the coronavirus, then?"
  • "Are you telling me it's cancer?"
  • "Could this be from the asbestos all those years ago?"
  • "Should I stop my blood pressure tablet?"

He goes quiet when he hears that it might be cancer, then asks whether his wife can come with him next time. He settles if the candidate is honest, unhurried and gives him a clear plan.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse, on room air throughout. Weight 68 kg today (practice record 74 kg eight months ago); height 178 cm. The 10:20 set was taken straight after he walked about 50 m to the treatment room.
handover.model:
Read: at rest at 10:05 and 15:10 his observations are within normal adult ranges: HR 84 to 86, RR 18, SpO2 95% on room air, BP 138 to 140/80 to 82, temperature 36.6 to 36.7 °C, alert. After a 50 m walk, SpO2 fell to 92%, HR rose to 98 and RR to 22, recovering at rest. Weight is down 6 kg (about 8%) in 8 months.

For Mr Davidson: his exertional breathlessness is real and objective, but he is stable, not hypoxic at rest and not septic. Unintentional loss of about 8% of body weight is a red flag.

What it changes: no adult observation chart applies in general practice. Nothing here calls for ambulance transfer, so he can have an urgent outpatient work-up with clear safety netting.

rows.note: Straight after walking about 50 m to the treatment room; coughing
On return from imaging, seated at rest

handover.label: Chest X-ray report
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA and lateral, erect.

Clinical details: 75-year-old man with a progressive dry cough for 4 to 5 months, exertional breathlessness, weight loss, hoarseness and dull upper right chest pain. Occupational asbestos exposure in the late 1960s and 1970s. Never smoker.

Comparison: no previous imaging available.

Technique: adequate inspiration, not rotated, adequately exposed.

Findings:

  • Lungs: a large, rounded soft-tissue opacity about 6 cm across in the right lung apex (right upper lobe), with a lobulated, ill-defined lower margin. It abuts the apical pleura. No cavitation. The rest of both lungs is clear, with no other nodule and no reticular or interstitial change.
  • Pleura: no pleural effusion. No pleural plaques or calcified pleural thickening. No pneumothorax.
  • Airway and mediastinum: trachea central and not deviated or narrowed. Mediastinum not widened. Both hila normal in size and position. Aortic arch normal.
  • Heart: cardiothoracic ratio below 0.5. Heart borders clear.
  • Diaphragm: both hemidiaphragms normal in position and outline. Costophrenic angles sharp. No free gas under the diaphragm.
  • Bones and soft tissues: no rib destruction is evident, but the posterior right first and second ribs are overlapped by the opacity and are not well assessed. Soft tissues normal.
  • Lines and devices: none.

Conclusion: right apical (superior sulcus) mass, highly suspicious for primary lung carcinoma. A pleural origin cannot be excluded on plain film. No pleural plaques, effusion or interstitial fibrosis is seen. Further evaluation with CT is suggested.
handover.model:
Spot diagnosis first: a large (about 6 cm) right upper lobe apical opacity, an apical (superior sulcus) lung tumour until proven otherwise.

Then systematically: correct patient and date, PA erect, not rotated, adequate inspiration and exposure. Soft tissues normal; no definite rib destruction, but the upper posterior ribs are hidden by the mass. Trachea central, mediastinum and hila normal, aortic arch normal. No other lung lesion, no reticular change, no effusion, no pleural plaques, no pneumothorax. Heart size normal. Diaphragms and costophrenic angles normal, no free gas. No lines. No other relevant findings beyond the mass.

For Mr Davidson: this fits his weight loss, dull upper right chest pain and hoarseness (an apical tumour can involve the right recurrent laryngeal nerve). It does not show asbestosis, plaques or an effusion, but plain film is insensitive for these. The mass abuts the pleura, so mesothelioma stays on the list.

What it changes: urgent contrast CT of the chest and upper abdomen, and urgent specialist referral for staging and tissue diagnosis.

handover.label: Blood results
handover.model:
Read: Hb 121 g/L with a normal MCV is a mild normocytic anaemia. Platelets 412 are mildly raised and WCC is normal. CRP 14 is mildly raised and albumin 33 is low. Sodium 137 and corrected calcium 2.42 are normal. Creatinine 92 with eGFR 70 is adequate for age. LFTs, including ALP, are normal.

For Mr Davidson: this picture of anaemia of chronic disease, reactive thrombocytosis, a low-grade inflammatory response and low albumin fits a malignancy and his weight loss. A normal white cell count with only a mild CRP rise makes bacterial infection unlikely. There is no hypercalcaemia or SIADH (paraneoplastic or metastatic), and normal LFTs give no evidence of liver involvement, although they do not exclude spread.

What it changes: renal function allows IV contrast for the CT, and these are baselines for the specialist team. Nothing here needs same-day hospital treatment.

labs.title: Urea, electrolytes, creatinine, calcium and liver function tests

ask: You are now calling the respiratory registrar at the local hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Mr Davidson, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Mr Davidson now, here in general practice.
Mr Davidson asks you what the X-ray shows and whether this is the coronavirus. What would you tell him, what warning signs would you give him, and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, third-year medical student at the practice, calling with my supervising GP. James Davidson, 75.
  • Situation: right apical lung mass on today's chest X-ray, suspicious for lung cancer. Requesting urgent review.
  • Background: 4 to 5 months of progressive dry cough and exertional breathlessness, 6 kg weight loss, hoarseness, dull upper right chest pain, lethargy. Builder through the late 1960s and 1970s with asbestos exposure. Never smoker. Hypertension on ramipril.
  • Assessment: stable, SpO2 95% at rest, 92% after a short walk. X-ray: 6 cm right apical mass abutting the pleura. Trachea, mediastinum, hila and heart normal. No effusion, plaques or fibrosis. Upper ribs not well seen. Bloods: mild normocytic anaemia, platelets 412, CRP 14, albumin 33. Calcium and sodium normal, eGFR 70. Likely primary lung cancer (superior sulcus); mesothelioma possible.
  • Recommendation: contrast CT chest and upper abdomen arranged. Please see him within 2 weeks and advise on staging.

Most likely: primary lung cancer, a right superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumour. For it: age 75, past asbestos exposure, progressive cough and breathlessness, about 8% weight loss, hoarseness, dull upper right chest pain, right apical dullness and a 6 cm apical mass on the X-ray. Against: never smoker, no haemoptysis.

  • Malignant mesothelioma: heavy asbestos exposure decades ago, chest pain, a mass abutting the pleura. Against: a discrete mass, no effusion or pleural thickening.
  • Asbestos-related pulmonary fibrosis (asbestosis): asbestos, dry cough, exertional dyspnoea. Against: no clubbing or crackles, no reticular change, does not explain the mass.
  • ACE inhibitor cough: dry cough on ramipril. Against: on it for years, does not explain weight loss or the mass.
  • Heart failure or TB: against: no orthopnoea or oedema, normal heart size; no fevers, sweats or travel, no cavitation.

1. Disposition: stable, not hypoxic at rest, no haemoptysis, stridor or facial swelling, so an urgent outpatient pathway. Discuss with the supervising GP today.
  2. Imaging: urgent contrast CT of the chest and upper abdomen (liver, adrenals). eGFR 70 allows contrast.
  3. Referral: phone and letter to a respiratory physician or lung cancer MDT, to be seen within 2 weeks (Optimal Care Pathway). Do not wait for the CT before referring. Include the asbestos history, X-ray and bloods.
  4. Do not delay: no antibiotics, and no trial off ramipril, in place of the work-up.
  5. Specialist work-up: PET-CT, tissue biopsy (CT-guided or bronchoscopic/EBUS), MRI for a superior sulcus tumour, and an MDT plan.
  6. Supportive care: symptoms, nutrition and weight. Involve his wife. Document the occupational exposure.

• In plain words: a shadow or lump at the top of the right lung that could be a cancer, possibly linked to his asbestos exposure; only a CT and a biopsy can tell for sure. No false reassurance, no definite diagnosis.
  • Coronavirus: very unlikely, as the cough built up over months without fever.
  • Understanding: checks it, invites questions, offers for his wife to come.
  • Red flags (at least three, each with its action):
    • severe or worsening breathlessness, or noisy breathing (stridor): 000
    • coughing up blood: 000 if more than a small amount, otherwise ED today
    • swelling of the face, neck or arm: ED today
    • new back or neck pain with weakness, numbness or tingling in the legs, or new trouble passing urine or controlling the bladder or bowels: call 000 or go to ED now
    New pain, weakness or numbness in the arm or hand: call the practice the same day.
  • Follow-up: GP review with the CT result within a week, with his wife there. Call the practice if he has not heard about the CT or specialist appointment.

ddx.dx: Primary lung carcinoma of the right superior sulcus (Pancoast tumour)
ddx.for: Age 75 with asbestos exposure in the late 1960s and 1970s, progressive dry cough and exertional breathlessness, 6 kg weight loss, hoarseness, dull upper right chest pain, right apical dullness and a 6 cm right apical mass on the chest X-ray.
ddx.against: He has never smoked and has had no haemoptysis.

ddx.for: Heavy asbestos exposure decades ago, chest pain, breathlessness and weight loss, with a mass abutting the apical pleura.
ddx.against: The X-ray shows a discrete apical mass with no pleural effusion, plaques or pleural thickening.

ddx.for: Asbestos exposure with a gradually progressive dry cough and exertional breathlessness.
ddx.against: No clubbing, no fine crackles, no reticular change on the X-ray, and it does not explain the mass.

ddx.for: A dry cough in a man taking ramipril.
ddx.against: He has taken it for years with no dose change, and it does not explain the breathlessness, weight loss, hoarseness or mass.

ddx.for: Age 75 with hypertension and exertional breathlessness.
ddx.against: No orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea or oedema, JVP not raised, and normal heart size on the X-ray.

ddx.for: An apical lung lesion with weight loss and lethargy.
ddx.against: No fevers, night sweats, travel or TB contact, and the lesion is a solid mass without cavitation.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Give the asbestos history only when the candidate asks specifically about asbestos, or about dust, fibres or hazardous materials at work. "What was your job?" alone does not release it. The source puts the dull chest pain in the upper left chest. Here it is on the upper right to agree with the right apical mass on the X-ray.

In Part 2, hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Mr Davidson puts his questions during the explanation if the candidate has not covered them. If he asks about his blood pressure tablet, a good answer is: "Don't stop it on your own, as your blood pressure still needs treating. It doesn't explain the shadow on the X-ray. Your GP may swap it for a similar tablet that doesn't cause cough, but that won't hold up the scan or the specialist." This answer is not marked. Credit the spot diagnosis and the systematic read of the X-ray (items 23 and 24) in the ISBAR assessment or the diagnosis answer. The source expects the spot diagnosis first, then a systematic read that finds nothing else relevant.

A high-performing candidate characterises the cough and picks up the weight loss, hoarseness, chest pain and the asbestos exposure, which needs a specific question. They screen for fibrosis, heart failure, COPD, infection and TB, and examine the neck nodes, the eyes for Horner's syndrome, and the lung apices. In Part 2 they give the spot diagnosis first, read the film systematically, and call this lung cancer until proven otherwise with mesothelioma as an alternative. They arrange an urgent CT and urgent specialist referral, explain the result honestly without false reassurance, and give specific red flags and follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes a generic cough history without asking about asbestos. They blame the ramipril or prescribe antibiotics, describe the X-ray without naming the mass, or reassure him that it is "probably nothing" or tell him outright that he has cancer.
explain:
Diagnosis: suspected lung cancer, a right superior sulcus tumour

Mr Davidson is 75 and was exposed to asbestos as a builder in the late 1960s and 1970s. He has a dry cough that has been getting worse for months, exertional breathlessness that stops him walking, unintentional weight loss, lethargy, a new hoarse voice and a dull, constant upper right chest pain. Each of these is a lung cancer symptom listed by Cancer Australia: a cough lasting more than 3 weeks or changing, breathlessness, chest or shoulder pain, weight loss, hoarseness and fatigue. Together they call for a chest X-ray. The X-ray shows a 6 cm right apical mass. In this context it is lung cancer until proven otherwise. Never having smoked lowers his risk but does not remove it: asbestos is itself a lung carcinogen, and its effect is multiplied in smokers.

Asbestos-related disease

  • Pleural plaques: the commonest marker of exposure, usually without symptoms.
  • Asbestosis: interstitial fibrosis, mainly in the lower zones. It causes a dry cough, exertional breathlessness, fine bibasal crackles and sometimes clubbing, and is confirmed on high-resolution CT.
  • Lung cancer: risk is increased after exposure, typically decades later.
  • Malignant mesothelioma: a pleural malignancy that usually appears decades after exposure, often with chest pain, breathlessness and a pleural effusion or pleural thickening.

A specific question about asbestos, or about dust and hazardous materials at work, is essential. "I was a builder" is not enough. Document the exposure, because it matters for the diagnosis and, once a diagnosis is made, for any compensation claim.

The superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumour

Tumours at the lung apex can invade the chest wall, the lower brachial plexus (C8 and T1), the sympathetic chain and nearby nerves. This causes shoulder and arm pain, weakness or numbness of the hand, and Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). They can also spread into the vertebral body or the intervertebral foramina and compress the spinal cord. On the right, the recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the subclavian artery near the apex, so involvement can cause hoarseness. Look for these features when an apical lesion is suspected. Apical masses are easy to miss on examination, so percuss above the clavicles.

Reading the chest X-ray

When a finding is obvious, state the spot diagnosis first, then read the film systematically so that nothing else is missed (DRSABCDE):

  • Details: name, date of birth, date, erect or supine.
  • RIPE: rotation, inspiration, projection, exposure.
  • Soft tissues and bones.
  • Airways and mediastinum: trachea, carina, mediastinal width, hila, aortic arch.
  • Breathing: lung fields, fissures, pleura, apices.
  • Circulation: heart size less than half the thoracic width, heart borders.
  • Diaphragm: levels, costophrenic angles, free gas.
  • Extras: lines, tubes, metalwork.

Here the only relevant finding is the right upper lobe apical mass. There are no plaques, effusion or fibrosis, but plain film is insensitive for early asbestosis and plaques, and it cannot reliably tell a peripheral lung tumour from a pleural one. Hence the CT.

The other results

The observations show an objective fall in saturation on exertion but a stable patient at rest. The bloods show a mild normocytic anaemia, reactive thrombocytosis, a mildly raised CRP and low albumin, in keeping with chronic disease. Calcium and sodium are normal, so there is no hypercalcaemia (bony metastases or a paraneoplastic effect) and no SIADH. Renal function allows contrast.

The differentials

  • Mesothelioma: must be considered with this exposure history, especially as the mass abuts the pleura. CT and biopsy will separate it from lung cancer.
  • Asbestosis: fits the exposure and the symptoms, but there are no crackles, clubbing or reticular change, and it does not explain the mass.
  • ACE inhibitor cough: a dry, tickly cough that usually settles within weeks of stopping the drug (eTG). Stopping the ACE inhibitor or swapping it for an angiotensin II receptor blocker is reasonable in any adult with a chronic cough, and can run alongside the urgent work-up. It must never replace or delay investigation of red flags.
  • Heart failure: against it are the absence of orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea and oedema, a normal JVP and a normal heart size.
  • COPD: unlikely in a never-smoker with no morning cough or wheeze.
  • Pneumonia: no fever, sputum or pleuritic pain.
  • TB: an apical lesion with weight loss always raises it, but he has no fevers, sweats, travel or contacts.
  • Coronavirus: does not cause a cough that builds steadily over months without fever.

Management in general practice (Optimal Care Pathway for people with lung cancer)

  • A suspicious chest X-ray needs an urgent contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and upper abdomen, and urgent referral to a respiratory physician or lung cancer multidisciplinary team, with the patient seen within 2 weeks. Do not let waiting for the CT delay the referral.
  • Do not give antibiotics or a trial off the ACE inhibitor in place of investigation.
  • The specialist team arranges staging (PET-CT, and MRI for a superior sulcus tumour), tissue diagnosis (CT-guided or bronchoscopic biopsy, EBUS for nodes) and an MDT plan.
  • The GP stays central: coordinating care, managing symptoms and nutrition, supporting the patient and family, and keeping track of results.

Communication and safety netting

Tell him honestly that the X-ray shows a lump that may be a cancer, that more tests are needed to be sure, and what happens next. Avoid both false reassurance and a premature diagnosis. Answer his coronavirus worry directly, check his understanding and invite his wife to the next visit. Red flags:

  • Call 000 for severe or worsening breathlessness, new noisy or high-pitched breathing (stridor, which in a man with a lung mass may mean the upper airway is being narrowed), new, severe or different chest pain, or coughing up more than a small amount of blood.
  • Call 000 or go to ED now for new back or neck pain with weakness, numbness or tingling in the legs, or new trouble passing urine or controlling the bladder or bowels (possible spinal cord compression from spread into the vertebral body or foramina).
  • Go to ED the same day for any blood in the phlegm, swelling of the face, neck or arm (superior vena cava obstruction), fever, or new confusion (for example hypercalcaemia).

These are oncological emergencies that need hospital assessment, not a routine GP visit. New pain, weakness or numbness in the arm or hand means the tumour may be involving the brachial plexus: it needs prompt review, so he should call the practice the same day, but it is not an emergency.

Book the GP review for the CT result, confirm that the specialist appointment is made, and ask him to call if he has not heard about either.
points: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks with weight loss, hoarseness, chest pain or breathlessness in an older adult needs a chest X-ray. A suspicious film needs an urgent CT and specialist referral, with the patient seen within 2 weeks.

Always ask specifically about asbestos and dust exposure at work. Asbestos causes pleural plaques, asbestosis, lung cancer and mesothelioma, often decades after exposure, and never having smoked does not exclude lung cancer.
When an X-ray finding is obvious, give the spot diagnosis first, then read the film systematically (DRSABCDE) to find what else is or is not there.
An apical (superior sulcus) tumour can cause shoulder and arm pain, hand weakness, Horner's syndrome and hoarseness, so examine the eyes, hands, neck nodes and lung apices.
ACE inhibitor cough is a diagnosis of exclusion. Never let a trial off ramipril, or a course of antibiotics, delay investigation of red-flag symptoms.
Explain a suspicious result honestly, without false reassurance or a premature diagnosis. Stridor or heavy haemoptysis means 000; SVC obstruction or signs of spinal cord compression mean urgent ED.
